sudo tar fvxz gfortran-4.8.2-darwin13.tar.bz2 -C /

Phil

messages.subject: Possible coef(mod, IRTpars = TRUE) calculation error
messages.subject_clean: Possible coef(mod, IRTpars = TRUE) calculation error
messages.body_plain:
Hi Phil,

I used an old version of MIRT until recently, and when I switched to version 1.21, my IRT coefficients are not being calculated correctly.  Here is some example code (my dataset has 12 items) that ran fine on ver 1.17.1:

mod3PLPost <- mirt(DCIcompPost,1, itemtype = '3PL', optimizer = 'NR', SE = TRUE, SE.type = "Louis")
coef3PLPost <- as.matrix(coef(mod3PLPost, IRTpars = TRUE, as.data.frame = TRUE))[1:48, ]
coef3PLPost <- matrix(as.vector(t(coef3PLPost)), nrow = 12, ncol = 12, byrow = TRUE)
colnames(coef3PLPost) <- c("Discr","Disc_2.5","Disc_97.5", "Diff","Diff_2.5","Diff_97.5", "Lower","Lower_2.5","Lower_97.5", "Upper", "Up_2.5","Up_97.5")
coef3PLPost[, c(1,4,7)]

However, with ver 1.21, a couple things seem to be happening.  1) The confidence intervals don't seem to be getting output as part of the coef() command (only the four main estimates).  2) The IRTpars = TRUE seems to have an error in the calculation for the typical IRT parameters (a, b,c).  Specifically, for the guessing parameter.  I know this becaus if you plot the model, the y-value for the item characteristic curves at low ability levels don't match the calculated guessing parameters (this is for ICCs that have flattened out at low ability levels).

Any ideas on what is happening?

Thanks,

Nick

messages.subject: computation time for different methods of fscores
messages.subject_clean: computation time for different methods of fscores
messages.body_plain:
Hi Phil,
Is there a reason why the computation time for WLE is substantially greater than other methods -- even with mirtCluster? It is understandable that WLE will take longer than Bayesian methods because for example EAP is relatively computationally simple than WLE. But it takes up to 5X longer even when compared to ML.
Cheers,
Alvin

library(mirt)
library(irtoys)
dataNRM <- as.data.frame(irtoys::Unscored)
mirtCluster()

NRMmod <- mirt(dataNRM, 1,
                  itemtype='nominal')

timeEAP <- system.time(fscores(NRMmod, method="EAP", full.scores = TRUE))
timeWLE <- system.time(fscores(NRMmod, method="WLE", full.scores = TRUE))
timeML <- system.time(fscores(NRMmod, method="ML", full.scores = TRUE))
timeMAP <- system.time(fscores(NRMmod, method="MAP", full.scores = TRUE))
print(c(timeEAP[3], timeWLE[3], timeML[3], timeMAP[3]))

mirtCluster(remove=TRUE)

messages.body_plain:
Hi Alvin,

On Thu, Jan 26, 2017 at 12:24 AM, Alvin <alv...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi Phil,
> Is there a reason why the computation time for WLE is substantially greater than other methods -- even with mirtCluster? It is understandable that WLE will take longer than Bayesian methods because for example EAP is relatively computationally simple than WLE. But it takes up to 5X longer even when compared to ML.

In addition to computing the likelihood at each iteration of the optimisation of theta, which is very easy, the Fisher information function for each item must also be computed at the same time, which grows as the number of items increases. As none of mirt's Fisher information functions are optimised with C++ code, and all of them are wrapped within slower S4 dispatch methods, there comes to be a lot of overhead. I can try and fix a bit of the S4 overhead, but rewriting all the Fisher information functions to C++ isn't really something I'm interested in doing any time soon (the payoff is really only seen in computing WLEs, everywhere else their requirement is basically trivial).

Phil

messages.subject: Re: computation time for different methods of fscores
messages.subject_clean: computation time for different methods of fscores
messages.body_plain:
On Thu, Jan 26, 2017 at 11:03 AM, Alvin <alv...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Thanks Phil!
> As an aside, would you think that the bias-reduction advantage of WLE over ML compensates for the computation time required? In very large datasets and multiple runs, the time difference can be substantial.

It can be, but to me this is generally a non-issue. The bias becomes reduced as the test length increases, so using WLE is not typically required here, and in smaller tests WLE still shouldn't take too long to obtain. So the trade-off doesn't seem all that bad.

On Thu, Jan 26, 2017 at 4:56 PM, Tyler Moore <reduct...@gmail.com> wrote:

>
> Hi Phil, I'm toying with one way to simulate NRM items without having to specify the response intercepts, and am getting some counter-intuitive results.  I was wondering if you might know why.  Here's the simulation script:
>
> library(psych)
> library(mirt)
>
> # Simulate a 20-item test with 10000 examinees using the basic 2PL.
> # All 20 items load 0.95 on a single factor, and difficulties range
> # from -1.5 to 1.5.  This results in a matrix of binary responses
> # (0 = incorrect; 1 = correct).
>
> x <- sim.structure(fx=matrix(0.95,20,1),items=TRUE,cat=1,d=round(runif(20,-1.5,1.5),0),n=10000)$observed
>
> # Now replace the incorrect responses (zeros) with random integers
> # between 2 and 5.  So when examinees get an item incorrect, they
> # do so by choosing some option other than 1.  Thus, the correct
> # answer to every item is 1, possible response options include
> # 1/2/3/4/5, and there are no distractor response options.
>
> for (i in 1:10000) {
> for (j in 1:20) {
> if (x[i,j] == 0) {x[i,j] <- round(runif(1,1.50001,5.49999),0)}
> }}
>
> # Estimate the NRM using 'mirt'
>
> mod <- mirt(x,1,itemtype="nominal")
>
> itemplot(mod,1)
>
> You'll notice that response option 1 (the correct response) has the opposite slope to what I was hoping - i.e. it looks like a person has to be low-ability before selecting 1.
>
> Now if I change the script to this (where 5 is the correct response and incorrect responses are random integers between 1 and 4), it seems to work fine:
>
> x <- sim.structure(fx=matrix(0.95,20,1),items=TRUE,cat=1,d=round(runif(20,-1.5,1.5),0),n=10000)$observed
>
> for (i in 1:10000) {
> for (j in 1:20) {
> if (x[i,j] == 1) {x[i,j] <- 5}
> if (x[i,j] == 0) {x[i,j] <- round(runif(1,0.5,4.49999),0)}
> }}
>
> mod <- mirt(x,1,itemtype="nominal")
>
> itemplot(mod,1)
>
> Any idea why results are different when all correct responses are 1?
>
> Thanks!
>
> Tyler

messages.subject: A bug with customK?
messages.subject_clean: A bug with customK?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Phil,

Thrilled to see you diligently maintaining this R package - what a great resource! Thank you.

I've got a possible error for you. I can't get the customK to work. I need to set the number of categories at 5 instead of 4, so that I can score a dataset that contains the same items but has more extreme scores. Here's an example that should throw an error. Can you explain what I'm doing wrong?

Thanks again.

dat <- Science - 1 #make all the categories go from 0-3
apply(dat, 2, table) #check it
calib <- mirt(dat, 1)
vals <- mod2values(calib)
vals$est <- FALSE
newdat <- dat
#change the number of categories from 4 to 5 on item 4:
newdat[2,4] <- 4
#This was the former customK:
 extract.mirt(calib, 'K')
#Now we want to update the number of categories to 5
customK <- c(4, 4, 4, 5)
newmod <- mirt(newdat, 1, pars=vals, technical = list(customK=customK))
#Throws an error:
#Error: Rows in supplied and starting value data.frame objects do not match. Were the
#             data or itemtype input arguments modified?

messages.subject: Re: A bug with customK?
messages.subject_clean: A bug with customK?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Charlie,

The problem is with your vals object. You are telling mirt that these are the starting values for the intercept/threshold parameters, in which given this information it understands that there are 4 categories (hence, 3 intercepts). However, you then tell it that there are really 5 categories, and therefore there should be a 4th intercept somewhere......except that there isn't. Hence, mirt knows you changed something in the pars object or data, because it doesn't match the information being generated internally.

So if you are going to edit the starting values/use customK, maybe start with the number of intercepts you need like this

> customK <- c(4, 4, 4, 5)

> vals <- mirt(newdat, 1, pars='values', technical = list(customK=customK))
> vals <- edit_the_values(vals)

> mod <- mirt(newdat, 1, pars=vals, technical = list(customK=customK))

HTH.

Phil
